topics.name: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
topics.summary: An angle is the amount of rotation of a ray from an initial to a terminal position, positive for anticlockwise and negative for clockwise rotation. Degree measure divides a full rotation into 360 equal parts; radian measure defines 1 radian as the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length equals the radius. Since a full rotation is \(2\pi\) radians and \(360^\circ\), the conversion is \(\pi \text{ rad} = 180^\circ\). The core relation linking arc length \(l\), radius \(r\) and angle \(\theta\) (in radians) subtended at the centre is \(l = r\theta\). This single formula underlies problems on wheel rotations, pendulum swings, and the length of an arc or a chord. Radian measure is always used in calculus and advanced trigonometry because it makes derivative and series formulas clean, so fluently converting between degrees and radians, and applying \(l=r\theta\) correctly (with \(\theta\) strictly in radians), is foundational for every later topic in the chapter.

worked_example.problem: Find the radian measure of \(40^\circ 20'\) and the length of an arc of a circle of radius 10 cm that subtends an angle of \(54^\circ\) at the centre.
worked_example.solution: First: \(40^\circ 20' = 40 + \tfrac{20}{60} = \tfrac{121}{3}\) degrees. Multiply by \(\tfrac{\pi}{180}\) to get \(\tfrac{121\pi}{540}\) radians. Second: convert \(54^\circ\) to radians: \(54 \times \tfrac{\pi}{180} = \tfrac{3\pi}{10}\). Apply \(l = r\theta = 10 \times \tfrac{3\pi}{10} = 3\pi\) cm \(\approx 9.42\) cm.

common_mistakes: Plugging a degree value directly into \(l=r\theta\) without first converting to radians.
Mixing up the conversion direction — multiplying by \(\tfrac{180}{\pi}\) when converting degrees to radians instead of \(\tfrac{\pi}{180}\).
Treating minutes and seconds as decimal fractions directly (e.g. reading \(40^\circ20'\) as \(40.2^\circ\) instead of \(40\tfrac{1}{3}^\circ\)).
Forgetting that radian measure is a pure (dimensionless) ratio, so mixing units of length inconsistently in arc-length problems.

topics.name: Trigonometric Functions — Signs, Domain & Range
topics.summary: For a point \(P(x,y)\) on a circle of radius \(r\) making angle \(\theta\) with the positive x-axis, the six trigonometric functions are defined as ratios: \(\sin\theta = y/r\), \(\cos\theta = x/r\), \(\tan\theta = y/x\), and their reciprocals \(\csc\theta, \sec\theta, \cot\theta\). Because \(x\) and \(y\) independently change sign across the four quadrants while \(r>0\) always, each function's sign follows the ASTC rule: All positive in Quadrant I, only Sine (and cosec) positive in II, only Tangent (and cot) positive in III, only Cosine (and sec) positive in IV. The domain of sine and cosine is all real numbers with range \([-1,1]\); tangent and secant are undefined wherever \(\cos\theta=0\) (i.e. odd multiples of \(\pi/2\)), and cotangent/cosecant are undefined wherever \(\sin\theta=0\) (integer multiples of \(\pi\)). Two Pythagorean identities, \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\), \(1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta\) and \(1+\cot^2\theta=\csc^2\theta\), tie all six functions together and are used constantly to simplify expressions and find one ratio from another.

worked_example.problem: If \(\cos\theta = -\tfrac{3}{5}\) and \(\theta\) lies in the third quadrant, find \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\).
worked_example.solution: Use \(\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta = 1 - \tfrac{9}{25} = \tfrac{16}{25}\), so \(\sin\theta = \pm\tfrac{4}{5}\). In the third quadrant only tangent (and cot) are positive, so sine must be negative: \(\sin\theta = -\tfrac{4}{5}\). Then \(\tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta = \tfrac{-4/5}{-3/5} = \tfrac{4}{5}\).

common_mistakes: Taking both square-root signs as valid answers without using the given quadrant to fix the sign.
Misremembering the ASTC order and its quadrants (e.g. thinking tangent is positive in Quadrant II).
Assuming \(\tan\theta\) is undefined at the same points as \(\sin\theta\) instead of where \(\cos\theta=0\).
Confusing the range of sine/cosine (bounded, \([-1,1]\)) with that of tangent (unbounded, all reals).

topics.name: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
topics.summary: Beyond the memorised table of standard angles (\(0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ\)), trigonometric ratios of any angle can be reduced to a ratio of an angle between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) using allied-angle identities — angles like \(90^\circ\pm\theta, 180^\circ\pm\theta, 270^\circ\pm\theta, 360^\circ\pm\theta\) and negative angles \(-\theta\). The reduction follows two simple rules: (1) for \(90^\circ\pm\theta\) and \(270^\circ\pm\theta\) (odd multiples of \(90^\circ\)), the function changes to its co-function (sine \(\leftrightarrow\) cosine, tan \(\leftrightarrow\) cot, sec \(\leftrightarrow\) cosec); for \(180^\circ\pm\theta\) and \(360^\circ\pm\theta\) (multiples of \(180^\circ\)), the function name stays the same. (2) the sign attached is whatever sign that same function would have in the quadrant the resulting angle falls in. Sine and tangent are odd functions (\(\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta\)), while cosine is even (\(\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta\)). Together with periodicity — sine and cosine repeat every \(2\pi\), tangent every \(\pi\) — these rules let any trigonometric value be evaluated exactly by hand.

worked_example.solution: Write \(210^\circ = 180^\circ + 30^\circ\). Since this is \(180^\circ+\theta\), the function name is unchanged and the sign is that of cosine in Quadrant III (negative): \(\cos(210^\circ) = -\cos 30^\circ = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\). For the second: \(\tan(-135^\circ) = -\tan(135^\circ)\) (tangent is odd). Now \(135^\circ = 180^\circ - 45^\circ\) gives \(\tan135^\circ = -\tan45^\circ = -1\), so \(\tan(-135^\circ) = -(-1) = 1\).

common_mistakes: Applying the co-function switch (sin \(\leftrightarrow\) cos) to \(180^\circ\pm\theta\) angles, where the function name should actually stay the same.
Getting the sign wrong by forgetting which quadrant the reduced angle actually lies in.
Treating cosine as an odd function like sine instead of remembering it is even.
Reducing \(270^\circ\pm\theta\) with the 'same function' rule instead of the co-function rule that odd multiples of \(90^\circ\) require.
Forgetting to first bring a large or negative angle within one period before applying an allied-angle rule, leading to an unnecessarily long reduction.

topics.name: Graphs of Trigonometric Functions
topics.summary: The graphs of \(y=\sin x\) and \(y=\cos x\) are smooth waves oscillating between \(-1\) and \(1\), each with period \(2\pi\); the cosine graph is simply the sine graph shifted left by \(\pi/2\). \(y=\tan x\) has period \(\pi\) and vertical asymptotes at odd multiples of \(\pi/2\) where it is undefined, with range all real numbers. The reciprocal graphs \(y=\csc x\) and \(y=\sec x\) consist of U-shaped branches that never enter the strip \((-1,1)\), with vertical asymptotes wherever sine (resp. cosine) is zero; \(y=\cot x\) behaves like a mirrored, shifted tangent graph with period \(\pi\). For a general form \(y = A\sin(Bx+C)+D\), the amplitude is \(|A|\), the period is \(2\pi/|B|\), the phase shift is \(-C/B\), and \(D\) shifts the whole graph vertically. Reading amplitude, period and shifts off a transformed graph, and knowing where each of the six basic graphs is zero, maximum, minimum or undefined, are the recurring skills tested on this topic.

worked_example.problem: State the amplitude, period and phase shift of \(y = 3\sin\!\big(2x - \tfrac{\pi}{3}\big)\)
worked_example.solution: Match to \(y=A\sin(Bx+C)\) with \(A=3, B=2, C=-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\). Amplitude \(=|A|=3\). Period \(=\dfrac{2\pi}{B}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\). Phase shift \(=-\dfrac{C}{B}=-\dfrac{-\pi/3}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (shift right by \(\pi/6\)).

common_mistakes: Reading off the period as \(2\pi/B\) without dividing by \(|B|\), giving a negative period when \(B\) is negative.
Confusing the graphs of tangent and cotangent, or misplacing their asymptotes.
Believing \(\csc x\) and \(\sec x\) have range \([-1,1]\) like sine and cosine, when in fact they exclude that entire interval.
Computing phase shift as \(C/B\) instead of \(-C/B\), flipping the direction of the shift.

topics.name: Sum and Difference Formulas (Compound Angles)
topics.summary: The compound-angle formulas express the sine, cosine and tangent of a sum or difference of two angles in terms of the individual angles' ratios: \(\sin(A\pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B\) and \(\cos(A\pm B) = \cos A\cos B \mp \sin A\sin B\) — note the sign flips between the two. Dividing sine by cosine gives the tangent addition formulas \(\tan(A\pm B) = \dfrac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A \tan B}\). These identities are the single most important toolkit in the chapter: they let you compute exact values of non-standard angles like \(15^\circ, 75^\circ, 105^\circ\) by writing them as a sum or difference of standard angles (e.g. \(75^\circ = 45^\circ+30^\circ\)), prove a wide range of identities, and they are the building blocks from which double-angle, triple-angle and transformation formulas are all derived by substitution (\(A=B\) gives double angle; further algebra gives sum-to-product). Mastery here makes every later topic in the chapter much faster.

worked_example.solution: Write \(75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ\) and apply the sine addition formula: \(\sin75^\circ = \sin45^\circ\cos30^\circ + \cos45^\circ\sin30^\circ\). Substitute the standard values: \(= \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\).

common_mistakes: Writing \(\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B\) — copying the sine formula's sign instead of flipping it for cosine.
Using \(+\) in the tangent-addition denominator instead of \(-\) (and vice-versa for difference).
Splitting a non-standard angle into a combination that doesn't actually use standard reference angles, making the computation unnecessarily hard.
Forgetting the tangent-addition formula is undefined when \(1\mp\tan A\tan B = 0\).

topics.name: Multiple and Sub-multiple Angle Formulas
topics.summary: Setting \(B=A\) in the compound-angle formulas produces the double-angle identities: \(\sin2A = 2\sin A\cos A\) and, using \(\sin^2A+\cos^2A=1\), three equivalent forms of \(\cos2A\): \(\cos^2A-\sin^2A\), \(2\cos^2A-1\), or \(1-2\sin^2A\) — choosing the right form to match what's given (pure sine or pure cosine) is a key exam skill. Further substitution with \(2A\) as a sum \(A+A+A\) gives the triple-angle formulas \(\sin3A = 3\sin A-4\sin^3A\) and \(\cos3A = 4\cos^3A-3\cos A\). Running the double-angle formulas in reverse with \(A\) replaced by \(A/2\) gives the half-angle (sub-multiple) formulas, e.g. \(\sin A = 2\sin\tfrac{A}{2}\cos\tfrac{A}{2}\) and \(\cos A = 1-2\sin^2\tfrac{A}{2}\). These formulas are indispensable for simplifying expressions, proving identities involving squared ratios, solving equations that mix an angle with its double or half, and for integration techniques met later in calculus. A frequent exam pattern gives one trigonometric ratio of a base angle and a quadrant, and asks for a ratio of the doubled or halved angle — this always reduces to picking the correctly signed form of the double- or half-angle identity above, so identifying which quadrant the target angle (not the base angle) lies in is the real skill being tested.

worked_example.problem: If \(\sin A = \tfrac{3}{5}\) with \(A\) acute, find \(\cos 2A\) and \(\sin 2A\).
worked_example.solution: Since \(A\) is acute, \(\cos A = \sqrt{1-\tfrac{9}{25}} = \tfrac{4}{5}\). Use \(\cos2A = 1-2\sin^2A = 1-2\cdot\tfrac{9}{25} = 1-\tfrac{18}{25} = \tfrac{7}{25}\). And \(\sin2A = 2\sin A\cos A = 2\cdot\tfrac{3}{5}\cdot\tfrac{4}{5} = \tfrac{24}{25}\).

common_mistakes: Using \(\cos2A = 1-2\sin^2A\) when the cosine value was given, instead of the more convenient \(2\cos^2A-1\) form (extra unnecessary steps, or sign slips from the unneeded square root).
Writing \(\sin2A = 2\sin A\) or \(\cos2A = 2\cos A\), dropping the second factor entirely.
Applying the half-angle sign ambiguity (\(\pm\)) without checking which quadrant \(A/2\) actually lies in.
Misremembering the triple angle formula's coefficient signs, e.g. writing \(\cos3A = 3\cos A - 4\cos^3A\) (swapping the sine and cosine triple-angle patterns).

topics.name: Transformation Formulas (Sum-to-Product & Product-to-Sum)
topics.summary: Transformation formulas convert products of sines/cosines into sums (and vice versa), which is essential for simplifying expressions and solving certain equations. From the compound-angle formulas, adding or subtracting pairs gives the product-to-sum identities, e.g. \(2\sin A\cos B = \sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)\). Running these in reverse, by substituting \(A=\tfrac{C+D}{2}, B=\tfrac{C-D}{2}\), gives the sum-to-product identities, e.g. \(\sin C+\sin D = 2\sin\tfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\tfrac{C-D}{2}\). There are four formulas in each direction, one for each combination of sine/cosine sum or difference, and they must be matched carefully since a sign error or swapped pair instantly produces a wrong identity. These identities are particularly useful for proving that a sum like \(\sin A+\sin B+\sin C\) under a triangle-angle condition factorises neatly, and for converting trigonometric equations of the form \(\sin C \pm \sin D = 0\) into a factored form that is easy to solve. Recognising when an expression is 'sum of two sines/cosines' versus 'product of two sines/cosines' — and picking the corresponding one of the eight formulas rather than trying to expand everything from scratch — is what separates a quick two-line simplification from a long, error-prone one.

worked_example.problem: Express \(\sin 70^\circ + \sin 10^\circ\) as a product and evaluate it.
worked_example.solution: Use \(\sin C+\sin D = 2\sin\tfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\tfrac{C-D}{2}\) with \(C=70^\circ, D=10^\circ\): \(= 2\sin40^\circ\cos30^\circ\). Since \(\cos30^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), this equals \(\sqrt3\,\sin40^\circ\) — a simplified closed form (numerically \(\approx 1.114\)).

common_mistakes: Mixing up which product-to-sum formula pairs with a \(+\) versus \(-\) on the right (e.g. using the \(2\sin A\cos B\) formula's sign pattern for \(2\cos A\sin B\)).
In the sum-to-product formulas, swapping the half-sum and half-difference arguments between the two factors.
Applying \(\cos C-\cos D = 2\sin\tfrac{C+D}{2}\sin\tfrac{C-D}{2}\) without the required leading negative sign (correct form has a \(-2\sin\tfrac{C+D}{2}\sin\tfrac{C-D}{2}\)).
Treating these as interchangeable with the double-angle formulas rather than a separate identity set.

topics.name: Trigonometric Equations
topics.summary: A trigonometric equation is solved for a general solution — infinitely many angles, expressed with an integer parameter \(n\in\mathbb{Z}\) — because trig functions are periodic. The three master results are: \(\sin\theta=\sin\alpha \Rightarrow \theta = n\pi + (-1)^n\alpha\); \(\cos\theta=\cos\alpha \Rightarrow \theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha\); and \(\tan\theta=\tan\alpha \Rightarrow \theta = n\pi+\alpha\). Solving a general equation usually means first reducing it to one of these three standard forms — via factoring, substituting a single variable like \(t=\sin\theta\) to get a quadratic, or applying an identity (double-angle, sum-to-product) to combine terms — and only then applying the matching general-solution formula. A frequent extra step is checking that a candidate value of, say, \(\sin\theta\) actually lies in \([-1,1]\) before accepting it, and excluding solutions that were introduced by squaring both sides or that make an original denominator zero. Where a restricted interval such as \([0,2\pi)\) is specified, the final step is always to substitute enough integer values of \(n\) into the general solution to list every value that falls inside that interval, neither missing one at the boundary nor over-including one just outside it.

worked_example.solution: Replace \(\sin^2\theta = 1-\cos^2\theta\): \(2(1-\cos^2\theta)+\sqrt3\cos\theta+1=0\), which simplifies to \(-2\cos^2\theta+\sqrt3\cos\theta+3=0\), i.e. \(2\cos^2\theta - \sqrt3\cos\theta - 3 = 0\). Factor: \((\cos\theta-\sqrt3)(2\cos\theta+\sqrt3)=0\). Since \(\cos\theta=\sqrt3\) is impossible (outside \([-1,1]\)), only \(\cos\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \cos\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\) is valid, giving \(\theta = 2n\pi \pm \tfrac{5\pi}{6},\ n\in\mathbb{Z}\).

common_mistakes: Giving only the principal-value solution instead of the full general solution with the integer parameter \(n\).
Using the wrong master formula for the reduced equation, e.g. applying the cosine pattern \(2n\pi\pm\alpha\) to a sine equation.
Accepting an extraneous root such as \(\cos\theta=\sqrt3\) or \(\sin\theta=2\) that lies outside \([-1,1]\).
Losing solutions by dividing both sides of an equation by a trig expression (like \(\sin\theta\)) that can itself be zero, instead of factoring.

questions.topic: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
questions.question: One full anticlockwise rotation of a ray back to its initial position measures:
questions.explanation: A complete rotation returns the ray to its starting position, which by definition measures \(360^\circ\) (equivalently \(2\pi\) radians).
questions.hint: Think of a clock's minute hand going all the way around once.
distractor_logic: Half of a full rotation, not the complete rotation.
Incorrectly claims degree measure cannot express a full rotation, when \(360^\circ\) and \(2\pi\) rad are simply two units for the same angle.
A quarter rotation, not a complete one.

questions.topic: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
questions.question: The radian is defined as the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length equals:
options: half the radius of the circle
questions.explanation: By definition, 1 radian is the angle subtended at the centre by an arc of length exactly equal to the radius \(r\).
questions.hint: Radius, not diameter — that's the key distinguishing word.
distractor_logic: Confuses radius with diameter; using the diameter would subtend twice this angle.
Half the radius gives an angle of \(0.5\) radian, not the defining case.
An arc equal to the full circumference subtends the entire \(2\pi\) rad, not 1 radian.

questions.topic: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
questions.question: The relation connecting degree and radian measure is:
questions.explanation: A straight angle, half of a full rotation, is \(180^\circ\) and also equals \(\pi\) radians, giving the standard conversion identity.
questions.hint: Picture a straight line — that's \(\pi\) radians and \(180^\circ\) at once.
distractor_logic: Understates the degree equivalent of \(\pi\) radians by half.
Mismatches \(2\pi\) (a full rotation) with only a quarter-turn in degrees.
Overstates the degree equivalent of \(\pi\) radians by double.

questions.topic: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
questions.question: For an arc of length \(l\) on a circle of radius \(r\) subtending angle \(\theta\) at the centre, the correct relation (with \(\theta\) in radians) is:
questions.explanation: The defining arc-length formula, valid only when \(\theta\) is measured in radians, is \(l=r\theta\).
questions.hint: It's a direct product of radius and (radian) angle, not a ratio or a sum.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly adds radius and angle instead of multiplying them.
Inverts the correct product relationship into a quotient.
Has radius and angle the wrong way round in the quotient.

questions.topic: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
questions.question: An angle is considered negative when the ray from its initial position rotates:
options: along the initial ray itself, without turning
questions.explanation: By the standard sign convention, anticlockwise rotation of the terminal ray is taken as positive and clockwise rotation as negative.
questions.hint: Anticlockwise is the positive convention; the other rotational direction is negative.
distractor_logic: This is the convention for a positive angle, the opposite of what's asked.
No rotation at all corresponds to a zero angle, not a negative one.
A \(180^\circ\) turn is a straight angle regardless of direction; the sign depends on the direction of rotation, not this specific magnitude.

questions.question: In which quadrant are all six trigonometric functions positive?
questions.explanation: The ASTC rule states 'All' functions are positive in Quadrant I, since both coordinates of a point there are positive.
questions.hint: Remember the mnemonic 'All Silver Tea Cups' for quadrants I, II, III, IV.
distractor_logic: In Quadrant II only sine (and cosecant) are positive, not all six.
In Quadrant III only tangent (and cotangent) are positive, not all six.
In Quadrant IV only cosine (and secant) are positive, not all six.

questions.question: The range of \(\cos\theta\) for real \(\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: Since cosine is the x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle, its value can never exceed 1 in magnitude, giving range \([-1,1]\), with both endpoints attained.
questions.hint: Cosine comes from a coordinate on the unit circle, so it's bounded on both sides.
distractor_logic: Cosine is bounded, not unbounded like tangent.
Cosine also takes negative values (e.g. \(\cos\pi=-1\)), so the range isn't restricted to non-negative numbers.
The endpoints \(\pm1\) ARE attained (e.g. at \(\theta=0,\pi\)), so the interval should be closed, not open.

questions.question: Which identity below is correct for all real \(\theta\)?
questions.explanation: The fundamental Pythagorean identity, following directly from the unit-circle definition \(x^2+y^2=r^2=1\), is \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\).
questions.hint: It comes from the equation of the unit circle itself.
distractor_logic: Has a sign error — subtracting instead of adding the two squared terms.
Confuses the identity with the (false, in general) statement that the un-squared ratios add to 1.
No such general identity exists; the product \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\) is not constantly 1.

questions.question: The function \(\tan\theta\) is undefined whenever:
questions.explanation: Since \(\tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta\), the function is undefined exactly where the denominator \(\cos\theta\) vanishes, i.e. at odd multiples of \(\pi/2\).
questions.hint: Look at what sits in the denominator of the tangent ratio.
distractor_logic: This is where cotangent (and cosecant) are undefined, not tangent.
This condition gives \(\tan\theta = 1\) (at \(\theta=\pi/4 + n\pi\)), a perfectly defined value, not an undefined point.
At \(\theta=0\), \(\tan\theta=0\) is perfectly well-defined.

questions.question: If \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III, which pair of functions is positive?
options: None of the six functions is positive
questions.explanation: By the ASTC rule, only Tangent (and its reciprocal, cotangent) is positive in Quadrant III; sine and cosine (and their reciprocals) are both negative there.
questions.hint: ASTC: Quadrant III is the 'T' quadrant.
distractor_logic: Sine and cosecant are negative in Quadrant III, not positive.
Cosine and secant are negative in Quadrant III, not positive.
Tangent and cotangent are in fact positive there, so it's incorrect to say none are.

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The exact value of \(\sin 30^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin30^\circ = \dfrac12\) is one of the standard values that should be memorised directly from the 30-60-90 triangle ratios.
questions.hint: This is the smallest non-zero value in the standard angle table.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\cos30^\circ\), not \(\sin30^\circ\).
This is the value of \(\sin45^\circ\) (or \(\cos45^\circ\)), not \(\sin30^\circ\).
This would be the value at \(90^\circ\), not \(30^\circ\).

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The exact value of \(\tan 60^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\tan60^\circ = \dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{\cos60^\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt3/2}{1/2} = \sqrt3\), a standard-table value.
questions.hint: It's the reciprocal of the value of \(\tan30^\circ\).
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\tan30^\circ\) — its reciprocal, not \(\tan60^\circ\) itself.
This is the value of \(\tan45^\circ\), not \(\tan60^\circ\).
Tangent is undefined at \(90^\circ\), not at \(60^\circ\), where cosine is nonzero.

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: Using the allied-angle rule, \(\sin(90^\circ - \theta)\) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Since \(90^\circ\) is an odd multiple of \(90^\circ\), the co-function rule applies and the sign is positive because \(90^\circ-\theta\) stays in Quadrant I for acute \(\theta\): \(\sin(90^\circ-\theta)=\cos\theta\).
questions.hint: Sine and cosine are co-functions of each other under this particular shift.
distractor_logic: Fails to apply the required co-function switch for a shift by an odd multiple of \(90^\circ\).
Applies the correct co-function switch but with the wrong sign.
Uses the correct co-function switch but incorrectly attaches a negative sign.

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The value of \(\cos 180^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: The point on the unit circle at angle \(180^\circ\) is \((-1,0)\), so \(\cos180^\circ = -1\).
questions.hint: This angle points along the negative x-axis on the unit circle.
distractor_logic: This is the value at \(0^\circ\), not \(180^\circ\).
This is the value of \(\sin180^\circ\) (the y-coordinate), not \(\cos180^\circ\).
Cosine is well-defined at every real angle, including \(180^\circ\); only tangent/secant have points of undefinedness.

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: Since sine is an odd function, \(\sin(-\theta)\) equals:
questions.explanation: An odd function satisfies \(f(-\theta) = -f(\theta)\); sine is odd, so \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\).
questions.hint: Odd function: negating the input negates the output.
distractor_logic: This would make sine an even function, but sine is odd.
This confuses sine with cosine, the even function among the two.
This attaches both the wrong sign and the wrong function name.

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The period of the sine function, i.e. the smallest positive \(T\) with \(\sin(\theta+T)=\sin\theta\) for all \(\theta\), is:
questions.explanation: Sine completes one full oscillation, returning to the same value, after a rotation of exactly \(2\pi\) radians (\(360^\circ\)).
questions.hint: This is the same as the angle measure of one complete rotation.
distractor_logic: This is the period of tangent and cotangent, not sine.
\(\sin(\theta+\pi/2)\neq\sin\theta\) in general, so this is too short to be the period.
While \(4\pi\) is indeed a period (any multiple of \(2\pi\) works), it is not the smallest one.

questions.question: The maximum value attained by \(y = \cos x\) is:
questions.explanation: The cosine graph oscillates between \(-1\) and \(1\), reaching its maximum value of \(1\) at \(x=0, 2\pi, \ldots\)
questions.hint: This is the same value as the amplitude of the basic cosine wave.
distractor_logic: This is the minimum value of cosine, not the maximum.
This is a value cosine passes through, not its peak value.
Cosine is in fact bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\), unlike tangent.

questions.question: The graph of \(y=\tan x\) has vertical asymptotes at:
options: nowhere — the graph has no asymptotes

questions.question: The general solution of \(\sin\theta = 0\) is:

questions.question: The exact value of \(\cos 105^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: Write \(105^\circ = 60^\circ+45^\circ\): \(\cos105^\circ = \cos60^\circ\cos45^\circ-\sin60^\circ\sin45^\circ = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} = \tfrac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}{4}\), which is negative since \(105^\circ\) is obtuse.
questions.hint: \(105^\circ\) is obtuse, so its cosine must come out negative — use that to check your final sign.
distractor_logic: Flips the sign of the correct value, making a negative quantity look positive.
This is the (positive) value of \(\sin75^\circ\), not the correctly-signed \(\cos105^\circ\).

questions.question: If \(\cos A=\tfrac45\) and \(\cos B=\tfrac{12}{13}\), with both \(A\) and \(B\) acute, then \(\cos(A-B)\) equals:
questions.explanation: \(\sin A=\tfrac35,\ \sin B=\tfrac{5}{13}\). Then \(\cos(A-B)=\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B = \tfrac45\cdot\tfrac{12}{13}+\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac{5}{13} = \tfrac{48}{65}+\tfrac{15}{65}=\tfrac{63}{65}\).
questions.hint: Find the missing sines first, then apply the cosine-of-difference formula (which uses a plus sign).
distractor_logic: Uses \(\cos(A+B)\)'s minus-sign pattern instead of the plus sign required for \(\cos(A-B)\).
Reports only the first product term (\(\cos A\cos B\)'s numerator) without adding the second.
Reports only the second product term (\(\sin A\sin B\)'s numerator) without adding the first.

questions.question: If \(\tan A = 2\) and \(\tan B = 3\), the value of \(\tan(A+B)\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\tan(A+B) = \dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B} = \dfrac{2+3}{1-6} = \dfrac{5}{-5} = -1\).
questions.hint: Compute numerator and denominator separately before dividing — the denominator here becomes negative.
distractor_logic: Flips the sign of the denominator (\(1+\tan A\tan B\) instead of \(1-\tan A\tan B\)), giving the wrong sign overall.
Reports the numerator alone, forgetting to divide by the denominator.
Reports the numerator with the wrong sign, forgetting to divide by the denominator.

questions.question: If \(\sin\theta = \tfrac35\) with \(\theta\) acute, the value of \(\sin2\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos\theta = \tfrac45\) (acute, so positive). Then \(\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 2\cdot\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac45 = \tfrac{24}{25}\).
questions.hint: Find cosine from the Pythagorean identity first, then double the product.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\cos2\theta\) (via \(1-2\sin^2\theta\)), not \(\sin2\theta\).
Forgets the required factor of 2 in the double-angle formula.
Simply doubles \(\sin\theta\) itself instead of applying the actual double-angle formula.

questions.question: If \(\cos\theta = \tfrac45\) with \(\theta\) acute, the value of \(\cos2\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: Using \(\cos2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta-1 = 2\cdot\tfrac{16}{25}-1 = \tfrac{32}{25}-1=\tfrac{7}{25}\).
questions.hint: Use the form of the double-angle formula written purely in terms of cosine.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\sin2\theta\), not \(\cos2\theta\).
Flips the sign of the correct result.
Forgets to subtract 1 after doubling \(\cos^2\theta\).

questions.question: If \(\tan\theta = \tfrac34\), the value of \(\tan2\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\tan2\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{2\cdot3/4}{1-9/16} = \dfrac{3/2}{7/16} = \dfrac{3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{16}{7} = \dfrac{24}{7}\).
questions.hint: Compute numerator and denominator of the double-angle tangent formula as separate fractions before dividing.
distractor_logic: Inverts the correct fraction.
Simply doubles \(\tan\theta\) directly, ignoring the required denominator entirely.
Correct magnitude but wrong sign — nothing in this computation should introduce a negative sign.

questions.question: If \(\sin A = \tfrac13\), the value of \(\cos2A\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos2A = 1-2\sin^2A = 1-2\cdot\tfrac19 = 1-\tfrac29=\tfrac79\).
questions.hint: Use the cosine double-angle form written purely in terms of sine.
distractor_logic: Forgets the leading 1, reporting only the subtracted term's numerator over 9.
Flips the sign of the correct result.

questions.question: Given \(\sin\theta=\tfrac12\) with \(\theta=30^\circ\), the value of \(\sin3\theta\) computed from \(3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin3\theta = 3\cdot\tfrac12 - 4\cdot\big(\tfrac12\big)^3 = \tfrac32-\tfrac12 = 1\), consistent with \(3\theta=90^\circ\) directly giving \(\sin90^\circ=1\).
questions.hint: Substitute the given value into the triple-angle formula carefully, then sanity-check against \(\sin90^\circ\).
distractor_logic: This is simply the given value of \(\sin\theta\) again, without actually applying the triple-angle formula.
Only the first term of the formula, forgetting to subtract \(4\sin^3\theta\).
An arithmetic slip that cancels the two terms entirely instead of correctly subtracting them.

questions.question: If \(\cos A = \tfrac{7}{25}\) with \(0<A<90^\circ\), the value of \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2}\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1-\cos A}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1-7/25}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{18/25}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{9}{25}} = \tfrac35\) (positive since \(0<A/2<45^\circ\)).
questions.hint: Apply the half-angle formula \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2}=\sqrt{(1-\cos A)/2}\) directly and simplify the fraction under the root.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\cos\tfrac{A}{2}\) (using the \(1+\cos A\) form), not \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2}\).
Repeats the given value of \(\cos A\) without applying the half-angle formula at all.
An intermediate, unsimplified fraction rather than the final simplified square-root value.

questions.question: \(\sin 40^\circ + \sin 20^\circ\) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Using \(\sin C+\sin D=2\sin\tfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\tfrac{C-D}{2}\) with \(C=40^\circ, D=20^\circ\): \(2\sin30^\circ\cos10^\circ = 2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\cos10^\circ = \cos10^\circ\).
questions.hint: Apply the sum-to-product formula first, then simplify using the standard value \(\sin30^\circ=\tfrac12\).
distractor_logic: Uses the half-difference angle where the half-sum angle should go, mixing up the two arguments.
Drops the constant factor \(2\sin30^\circ=1\) that simplifies the expression to exactly \(\cos10^\circ\), leaving an extra loose term.

questions.question: \(2\cos 50^\circ \sin 10^\circ\) is equal to:
questions.explanation: Using \(2\cos A\sin B = \sin(A+B)-\sin(A-B)\) with \(A=50^\circ, B=10^\circ\): \(\sin60^\circ-\sin40^\circ\).
questions.hint: This product matches the \(2\cos A\sin B\) pattern, which converts to a difference of sines.
distractor_logic: Uses the sum instead of the required difference for this particular product-to-sum pattern.
This is the identity pattern for \(2\cos A\cos B\), involving cosine terms, not \(2\cos A\sin B\).
Wrong function (cosine instead of sine) and wrong sign (sum instead of difference).

questions.question: \(\sin 50^\circ - \sin 10^\circ\) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Using \(\sin C-\sin D=2\cos\tfrac{C+D}{2}\sin\tfrac{C-D}{2}\) with \(C=50^\circ, D=10^\circ\): \(2\cos30^\circ\sin20^\circ = 2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\sin20^\circ = \sqrt3\sin20^\circ\).
questions.hint: Apply the sine-difference-to-product formula, then substitute the standard value \(\cos30^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
distractor_logic: Swaps cosine for sine in the constant factor, changing \(\sqrt3\) into a cosine-based value instead.
Drops the constant factor \(\sqrt3\) that comes from \(2\cos30^\circ\), replacing it with a plain 2.
Loses the constant factor from \(2\cos30^\circ\) altogether.

questions.question: \(\cos 70^\circ + \cos 50^\circ\) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Using \(\cos C+\cos D=2\cos\tfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\tfrac{C-D}{2}\) with \(C=70^\circ, D=50^\circ\): \(2\cos60^\circ\cos10^\circ = 2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\cos10^\circ = \cos10^\circ\).
questions.hint: Apply the cosine-sum-to-product formula, then use the standard value \(\cos60^\circ=\tfrac12\).
distractor_logic: Confuses this with a sine-based identity instead of the correct cosine-based one.
Leaves the loose constant factor without simplifying it against the \(\cos10^\circ\) term.
Loses the \(\cos10^\circ\) factor, keeping only a constant.

questions.question: The general solution of \(2\sin\theta - 1 = 0\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin\theta=\tfrac12=\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), so applying the sine master formula: \(\theta=n\pi+(-1)^n\tfrac{\pi}{6}\).
questions.hint: Isolate \(\sin\theta\) first, recognise it as a standard value, then apply the sine general-solution pattern.
distractor_logic: Applies the cosine master-formula pattern instead of the correct sine one.
Applies the tangent master-formula pattern instead of the correct sine one.

questions.question: The general solution of \(\sqrt3\tan\theta - 1 = 0\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\tan\theta = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} = \tan\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), so applying the tangent master formula: \(\theta=n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{6}\).
questions.hint: Isolate \(\tan\theta\) first, recognise the standard value, then apply the (simplest) tangent general-solution pattern.

questions.question: The general solution of \(2\cos\theta + 1 = 0\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos\theta = -\tfrac12 = \cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\), so applying the cosine master formula: \(\theta = 2n\pi \pm \tfrac{2\pi}{3}\).
questions.hint: Recognise \(-\tfrac12\) as \(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\) (an obtuse reference angle), then apply the cosine general-solution pattern.
distractor_logic: Applies the sine master-formula pattern instead of the correct cosine one.

questions.question: Solving \(\sin2\theta = \sin\theta\) by factoring gives \(\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)=0\). The full solution set is:
questions.explanation: Setting each factor to zero: \(\sin\theta=0 \Rightarrow \theta=n\pi\), and \(\cos\theta=\tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta=2n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{3}\). Both families together form the complete solution set.
questions.hint: Both factors can independently be zero — combine both resulting families, don't pick only one.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the family from the first factor, missing the solutions where \(\cos\theta=\tfrac12\).
Keeps only the family from the second factor, missing the solutions where \(\sin\theta=0\).

questions.question: The general solution of \(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \tfrac12\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta = \cos2\theta\), so \(\cos2\theta=\tfrac12=\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}\) gives \(2\theta=2n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{3}\), i.e. \(\theta = n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{6}\) after dividing by 2.
questions.hint: Recognise the left side as the double-angle formula for cosine before applying the master formula — remember to divide the final answer by 2 as well.
distractor_logic: Forgets to divide the leading \(2n\pi\) term by 2 along with the reference-angle term, only halving the latter.

Divides the reference angle by 2 but forgets the original reference angle should have been \(\pi/3\), not \(\pi/6\), before that division.

questions.question: The general solution of \(\tan^2\theta = 3\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\tan\theta = \pm\sqrt3\). \(\tan\theta=\sqrt3\) gives \(\theta=n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{3}\), and \(\tan\theta=-\sqrt3\) gives \(\theta=n\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\); combined, \(\theta=n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{3}\).
questions.hint: Taking the square root gives two cases for \(\tan\theta\) — solve each with the tangent master formula and combine.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the positive-root family, missing the solutions from \(\tan\theta=-\sqrt3\).

questions.question: Solving \(2\cos^2\theta + 3\sin\theta - 3 = 0\) by substituting \(\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta\) reduces it to \(2\sin^2\theta - 3\sin\theta + 1 = 0\), which factors as \((2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta-1)=0\). The possible values of \(\sin\theta\) are:
questions.explanation: Setting each factor to zero: \(2\sin\theta-1=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=\tfrac12\), and \(\sin\theta-1=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=1\). Both roots are within \([-1,1]\), so both are valid.
questions.hint: A quadratic in \(\sin\theta\) has two roots — check both lie within \([-1,1]\) before combining their general solutions.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the first factor's root, discarding the equally valid \(\sin\theta=1\) solution.

questions.topic: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
questions.question: Two concentric circles have radii 20 cm and 10 cm. An arc of the outer circle of length 30 cm subtends a certain angle at the common centre. The length of the arc of the inner circle subtending the same angle is:
questions.explanation: The common angle is \(\theta = l_{\text{outer}}/r_{\text{outer}} = 30/20 = 1.5\) rad. The inner arc is then \(l_{\text{inner}} = r_{\text{inner}}\theta = 10 \times 1.5 = 15\) cm.
questions.hint: First find the shared angle from the outer circle's data, then reapply \(l=r\theta\) with the inner radius.
distractor_logic: Multiplies the outer arc length by the ratio of radii the wrong way round (doubling instead of halving).
Repeats the outer radius' value as if it were the inner arc length.

questions.topic: Angles and Their Measurement (Degrees, Radians, Arc Length)
questions.question: A wheel of radius 0.25 m makes 5 complete revolutions per second. The linear speed of a point on its rim is:
questions.explanation: Angular speed \(\omega = 5 \times 2\pi = 10\pi\) rad/s. Linear speed \(v=r\omega = 0.25 \times 10\pi = 2.5\pi\) m/s.
questions.hint: First convert revolutions per second into radians per second, then apply \(v=r\omega\).
distractor_logic: Uses the radius alone without multiplying by the angular speed at all.
Uses only the number of revolutions per second (5) instead of the full angular speed \(10\pi\).
Doubles the correct answer by forgetting to include the radius factor of 0.25.

questions.question: If \(\tan\theta + \cot\theta = 2\), the value of \(\sin2\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\tan\theta+\cot\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \dfrac{2}{\sin2\theta}\). Setting this equal to 2 gives \(\sin2\theta = 1\).
questions.hint: Combine the two ratios over a common denominator and recognise the Pythagorean identity in the numerator.
distractor_logic: Confuses the given sum (2) directly with the value of \(\sin2\theta\) without doing the algebra.
Stops one step early, reporting \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\)'s reciprocal-equation constant instead of solving for \(\sin2\theta\).
An arithmetic slip that produces a value outside the valid range check by coincidence-free reasoning.

questions.question: If \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \dfrac15\) and \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II, the value of \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: Squaring, \(1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \tfrac{1}{25}\) gives \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = -\tfrac{12}{25}\). Then \((\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^2 = 1-2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1+\tfrac{24}{25} = \tfrac{49}{25}\), so \(\sin\theta-\cos\theta = \pm\tfrac75\); in Quadrant II sine is positive and cosine is negative, so the difference is positive: \(\tfrac75\).
questions.hint: Square the given sum to extract \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\) first, then build \((\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^2\) from it.
distractor_logic: Correct magnitude but wrong sign — in Quadrant II, \(\sin\theta>0>\cos\theta\), so the difference must be positive.
Reports \((\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^2\) itself (a squared quantity) instead of taking its square root.
Simply repeats the given value of \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta\) without doing any of the required algebra.

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The value of \(\sin 600^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: \(600^\circ - 360^\circ = 240^\circ = 180^\circ+60^\circ\), so \(\sin600^\circ = \sin240^\circ = -\sin60^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) (sine negative in Quadrant III).
questions.hint: First subtract a full rotation to bring the angle within \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\), then reduce further.
distractor_logic: Drops the required negative sign — the reduced angle \(240^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III, where sine is negative.
Uses the reference angle \(30^\circ\) instead of the correct \(60^\circ\).
Combines the wrong reference angle (\(30^\circ\)) with the wrong sign as well.

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The value of \(\cos(-1470^\circ)\) is:
questions.explanation: Since cosine is even, \(\cos(-1470^\circ)=\cos1470^\circ\). Subtracting \(4\times360^\circ=1440^\circ\) leaves \(30^\circ\), so the value is \(\cos30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
questions.hint: Use cosine's even-function property first, then reduce the large angle by removing full rotations of \(360^\circ\).
distractor_logic: Correctly reduces the angle but incorrectly attaches a negative sign, forgetting cosine is positive in Quadrant I.
This is the value of \(\sin30^\circ\) (using the wrong function), not \(\cos30^\circ\).

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The value of \(\tan\dfrac{19\pi}{3}\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\tfrac{19\pi}{3} - 6\pi = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\) (removing three full rotations, using tangent's period of \(\pi\) even more directly: \(\tfrac{19\pi}{3}\bmod\pi = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\)). So \(\tan\tfrac{19\pi}{3} = \tan\tfrac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt3\).
questions.hint: Tangent repeats every \(\pi\), not just every \(2\pi\) — reduce using the shorter period for a faster solution.

Uses the reciprocal ratio (cotangent's value at this angle) instead of tangent's.

questions.question: The graph of \(y = 2\sin\!\big(2x - \tfrac{\pi}{3}\big)\) attains a local maximum at \(x =\):
questions.explanation: A maximum occurs where the argument equals \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(2x-\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\tfrac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow 2x = \tfrac{5\pi}{6} \Rightarrow x=\tfrac{5\pi}{12}\).
questions.hint: Set the entire argument of sine, not just \(x\) itself, equal to \(\pi/2\), then solve for \(x\).
distractor_logic: Sets only the phase-shift term \(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\) (divided incorrectly) equal to the maximum condition, without properly solving the full equation.
This is where the argument itself (not \(x\)) would equal \(\pi/6\), an intermediate slip.

questions.question: The minimum value of \(y = 3\cos x - 4\), and the smallest positive \(x\) (in \([0,2\pi]\)) at which it occurs, are:
questions.explanation: \(\cos x\) attains its minimum value \(-1\) at \(x=\pi\), giving \(y = 3(-1)-4 = -7\).
questions.hint: Find where the underlying cosine term is smallest first, then substitute into the full expression.
distractor_logic: Forgets to include the vertical shift of \(-4\), reporting only the minimum of \(3\cos x\) itself.
Uses the location of cosine's maximum (\(x=0\)) instead of its minimum (\(x=\pi\)).

questions.question: If \(\sin A = \tfrac35\) with \(A\) acute, and \(\cos B = -\tfrac{12}{13}\) with \(B\) obtuse, then \(\sin(A+B)\) equals:
questions.explanation: \(\cos A=\tfrac45\) (A acute). Since B is obtuse, \(\sin B = +\tfrac{5}{13}\) (sine positive in Quadrant II). Then \(\sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B = \tfrac35\!\left(-\tfrac{12}{13}\right)+\tfrac45\!\cdot\!\tfrac{5}{13} = -\tfrac{36}{65}+\tfrac{20}{65} = -\tfrac{16}{65}\).
questions.hint: Carefully fix the sign of \(\sin B\) from B's quadrant (obtuse means Quadrant II, where sine is still positive) before substituting.
distractor_logic: Correct magnitude but wrong sign — likely from incorrectly taking \(\sin B\) as negative.

questions.question: If \(A+B = 45^\circ\), the value of \((1+\tan A)(1+\tan B)\) is:
options: cannot be determined without knowing \(A\) and \(B\) individually
questions.explanation: Since \(\tan(A+B) = \tan45^\circ = 1\), the formula \(\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}=1\) rearranges to \(\tan A+\tan B+\tan A\tan B = 1\). Expanding \((1+\tan A)(1+\tan B) = 1+\tan A+\tan B+\tan A\tan B = 1+1 = 2\) — independent of the individual values of \(A\) and \(B\).
questions.hint: Expand the product and compare it to the rearranged tangent-addition formula at \(A+B=45^\circ\).
distractor_logic: Drops the leading \(1\) from the expansion of the product, reporting only \(\tan A+\tan B+\tan A\tan B\).

questions.question: The exact value of \(\sin 15^\circ \cos 15^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: Recognise this as half the double-angle formula: \(\sin15^\circ\cos15^\circ = \tfrac12\sin30^\circ = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac14\).

questions.question: If \(\tan A = \tfrac12\) and \(\tan B = \tfrac13\), with \(A\) and \(B\) both acute, then \(A+B\) equals:

questions.hint: Compute \(\tan(A+B)\) first from the addition formula, then identify the standard angle it corresponds to.

questions.question: The value of \(\cos75^\circ\cos15^\circ - \sin75^\circ\sin15^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: This matches the pattern \(\cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B = \cos(A+B)\) with \(A=75^\circ, B=15^\circ\): \(\cos(75^\circ+15^\circ) = \cos90^\circ = 0\).

questions.question: If \(\cos A = -\tfrac35\) with \(90^\circ<A<180^\circ\), the value of \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2}\) is:
questions.explanation: Since \(45^\circ<A/2<90^\circ\) (Quadrant I), \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2}=+\sqrt{\tfrac{1-\cos A}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1+3/5}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{8/5}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac45} = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt5} = \tfrac{2\sqrt5}{5}\).

An unsimplified or miscalculated intermediate value rather than the correct final radical.

questions.question: Continuing from the same data (\(\cos A=-\tfrac35\), \(90^\circ<A<180^\circ\)), the value of \(\cos\tfrac{A}{2}\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos\tfrac{A}{2} = +\sqrt{\tfrac{1+\cos A}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1-3/5}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{2/5}{2}} = \sqrt{\tfrac15} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5} = \tfrac{\sqrt5}{5}\) (positive, since \(A/2\) is in Quadrant I).
questions.hint: Use the \(1+\cos A\) half-angle form for cosine this time, keeping the same positive sign reasoning as before.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2}\), not \(\cos\tfrac{A}{2}\) — the two half-angle values have been swapped.
Correct magnitude but wrong sign, despite \(A/2\) lying in Quadrant I where cosine is positive.
An incorrectly simplified radical rather than the correctly reduced \(\sqrt5/5\).

questions.question: If \(\sin\theta = \tfrac13\) with \(\theta\) acute, the value of \(\cos3\theta\) (using \(\cos3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta\)) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1-\tfrac19} = \tfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}\). Then \(\cos3\theta = 4\!\left(\tfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}\right)^{\!3} - 3\!\cdot\!\tfrac{2\sqrt2}{3} = \tfrac{64\sqrt2}{27}-\tfrac{54\sqrt2}{27} = \tfrac{10\sqrt2}{27}\).
questions.hint: Find \(\cos\theta\) first, then substitute carefully into the triple-angle formula — cube the fraction fully before subtracting.
distractor_logic: Forgets to cube the denominator of \(\cos\theta\) when computing \(\cos^3\theta\), inflating the first term.
Flips the sign of the correct result.
Makes an arithmetic slip subtracting the two terms of the triple-angle formula.

questions.question: If \(\tan\theta = \tfrac43\) with \(\theta\) acute, the value of \(\tan\tfrac{\theta}{2}\) (using \(\tan\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\)) is:
questions.explanation: From the \(3\text{-}4\text{-}5\) triangle, \(\sin\theta=\tfrac45,\ \cos\theta=\tfrac35\). Then \(\tan\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1-3/5}{4/5} = \dfrac{2/5}{4/5} = \dfrac12\).
questions.hint: Find sine and cosine from the given tangent value first (a 3-4-5 triangle), then substitute into the half-angle tangent formula.
distractor_logic: Inverts the correct fraction.
This is the value of \(\tan\theta\) itself divided differently, not \(\tan\tfrac{\theta}{2}\) from the correct formula.
Simply repeats the given value of \(\tan\theta\) without applying the half-angle formula at all.

questions.question: If \(\cos2\theta = \tfrac{7}{25}\) and \(\theta\) is acute, the value of \(\cos\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: Using \(\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1\): \(\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1+7/25}{2} = \dfrac{32/25}{2} = \dfrac{16}{25}\), so \(\cos\theta = \dfrac45\) (positive since \(\theta\) is acute).
questions.hint: Work backwards from the double-angle formula: rearrange it to isolate \(\cos^2\theta\) first, then take a square root.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\sin\theta\) (from the complementary computation), not \(\cos\theta\).
Simply repeats the given value of \(\cos2\theta\) without solving for \(\cos\theta\) at all.
Reports the intermediate value \(\cos^2\theta\) itself instead of taking its square root.

questions.question: The value of \(\cos40^\circ + \cos80^\circ + \cos160^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: Group the first two terms: \(\cos40^\circ+\cos80^\circ = 2\cos60^\circ\cos20^\circ = \cos20^\circ\) (since \(\cos60^\circ=\tfrac12\)). Adding the third term: \(\cos20^\circ + \cos160^\circ = \cos20^\circ - \cos20^\circ = 0\) (since \(\cos160^\circ = \cos(180^\circ-20^\circ) = -\cos20^\circ\)).
questions.hint: Combine two of the three terms with a sum-to-product formula first, then use an allied-angle rule on what remains.
distractor_logic: Only combines two of the three terms and stops, missing the further simplification that makes the whole sum vanish.
An arithmetic slip in applying the allied-angle rule for \(\cos160^\circ\).
Same type of sign slip but landing on the negative of the actually-cancelling structure.

questions.question: The value of \(\sin20^\circ\sin40^\circ\sin80^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: This is a standard identity: \(\sin\theta\sin(60^\circ-\theta)\sin(60^\circ+\theta) = \tfrac14\sin3\theta\) with \(\theta=20^\circ\) gives \(\tfrac14\sin60^\circ = \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{8}\).
questions.hint: This matches the special triple-product identity \(\sin\theta\sin(60^\circ-\theta)\sin(60^\circ+\theta)=\tfrac14\sin3\theta\) — check that \(20^\circ, 40^\circ, 80^\circ\) fit the \(\theta, 60^\circ-\theta, 60^\circ+\theta\) pattern.
distractor_logic: This is the value of the analogous cosine product \(\cos20^\circ\cos40^\circ\cos80^\circ\), not the sine product.
Missing the factor of \(\sqrt3\) that comes from \(\sin60^\circ\) in the identity.
Overstates the correct value by a factor of \(\sqrt3\).

questions.question: The value of \(\cos20^\circ\cos40^\circ\cos80^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: This is a standard identity: \(\cos\theta\cos(60^\circ-\theta)\cos(60^\circ+\theta) = \tfrac14\cos3\theta\) with \(\theta=20^\circ\) gives \(\tfrac14\cos60^\circ = \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac18\).
questions.hint: Same special triple-product pattern as the sine version, but using \(\cos3\theta\) in place of \(\sin3\theta\).
distractor_logic: This is the value of the analogous sine product \(\sin20^\circ\sin40^\circ\sin80^\circ\), not the cosine product.
Forgets to apply the factor of \(\tfrac14\) from the identity, using \(\cos60^\circ\) alone.
Uses \(\tfrac{1}{4}\times\tfrac{1}{4}\) instead of the single factor of \(\tfrac14\) the identity actually requires.

questions.question: The expression \(\dfrac{\sin5x+\sin3x}{\cos5x+\cos3x}\) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: By sum-to-product, \(\sin5x+\sin3x=2\sin4x\cos x\) and \(\cos5x+\cos3x=2\cos4x\cos x\); the common factor \(2\cos x\) cancels, leaving \(\dfrac{\sin4x}{\cos4x}=\tan4x\).
questions.hint: Apply sum-to-product to numerator and denominator separately — both produce a common \(\cos x\) factor that cancels cleanly.
distractor_logic: Uses the half-difference angle (\(x\)) instead of the half-sum angle (\(4x\)) that survives after cancellation.
Doubles the correct angle, from forgetting that the \(2\cos x\) factors (not the whole numerator/denominator) are what cancel.
Uses the reciprocal function (cotangent instead of tangent) despite the ratio being sine-over-cosine, not cosine-over-sine.

questions.question: The general solution of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt2\) is:
questions.explanation: Write \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta = \sqrt2\sin\!\big(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big)\). The equation becomes \(\sin\!\big(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big) = 1\), whose general solution is \(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 2n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), giving \(\theta = 2n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\).
questions.hint: Rewrite the left side in the single-wave form \(R\sin(\theta+\phi)\) first — here \(R=\sqrt2\) and \(\phi=\pi/4\) — since the maximum value 1 for sine pins down a unique family.
distractor_logic: Uses tangent's \(n\pi\) spacing pattern instead of the correct \(2n\pi\) spacing that this sine equation (with a unique maximum condition) requires.
Introduces a spurious \(\pm\) as if this were a cosine equation with two solution families, when in fact \(\sin(\cdot)=1\) has only one per period.
Solves the related but different equation \(\sin(\theta+\pi/4) = 0\) instead of \(=1\).

questions.question: The general solution of \(\cos\theta - \sin\theta = 1\) is:
questions.explanation: Write \(\cos\theta-\sin\theta = \sqrt2\cos\!\big(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big)\). The equation becomes \(\cos\!\big(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\big) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), giving \(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 2n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{4}\), i.e. \(\theta = 2n\pi\) or \(\theta = 2n\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) (equivalently \(2n\pi+\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\)).
questions.hint: Rewrite the left side as \(R\cos(\theta+\phi)\) with \(R=\sqrt2,\ \phi=\pi/4\), then apply the cosine master formula to the shifted angle.
distractor_logic: This is the general solution to the different equation \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\), not \(\cos\theta-\sin\theta=1\).
Assumes only \(\theta=0\) and its full-rotation repeats solve the equation, missing the second family entirely.
Introduces a spurious \(\pm\pi/2\) pattern that doesn't correspond to either actual solution family.

questions.question: Solving \(\sin4\theta = \sin2\theta\) by writing it as \(2\cos3\theta\sin\theta = 0\) (via sum-to-product), the complete solution set is:
questions.explanation: Setting each factor to zero: \(\cos3\theta=0 \Rightarrow 3\theta=(2n+1)\tfrac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\tfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{6}\), and \(\sin\theta=0 \Rightarrow \theta=n\pi\). Both families together form the complete solution set.
questions.hint: This factored equation has two independent factors — solve each and combine both resulting families.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the family from the cosine factor, missing the solutions where \(\sin\theta=0\).
Keeps only the family from the sine factor, missing the solutions where \(\cos3\theta=0\).
An incorrect single family that doesn't match either factor's actual general solution.

questions.question: Solving \(\cos2\theta = \sin\theta\) by substituting \(\cos2\theta = 1-2\sin^2\theta\) reduces it to \(2\sin^2\theta + \sin\theta - 1 = 0\), which factors as \((2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+1)=0\). The possible values of \(\sin\theta\) are:
questions.explanation: Setting each factor to zero: \(2\sin\theta-1=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=\tfrac12\), and \(\sin\theta+1=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=-1\). Both roots lie within \([-1,1]\), so both are valid.
questions.hint: A quadratic in \(\sin\theta\) has two roots — check both lie within \([-1,1]\) before combining their general solutions.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the root from the first factor, discarding the equally valid \(\sin\theta=-1\) solution.
Keeps only the root from the second factor, discarding the equally valid \(\sin\theta=\tfrac12\) solution.
Reports the wrong sign for the second root — solving \(\sin\theta+1=0\) gives \(\sin\theta=-1\), not \(+1\).

questions.question: Solving \(\sin3\theta = \sin\theta\) by writing it as \(2\cos2\theta\sin\theta = 0\) (via sum-to-product), the complete solution set is:
questions.explanation: Setting each factor to zero: \(\cos2\theta=0 \Rightarrow 2\theta=(2n+1)\tfrac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\tfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{4}\), and \(\sin\theta=0 \Rightarrow \theta=n\pi\). Both families together form the complete solution set.
questions.hint: As with the similar \(\sin4\theta=\sin2\theta\) problem, both independent factors must be solved and combined.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the family from the cosine factor, missing the solutions where \(\sin\theta=0\).
Keeps only the family from the sine factor, missing the solutions where \(\cos2\theta=0\).
Uses the wrong period in the combined family, mismatching the actual spacing between zeros of \(\cos2\theta\).

questions.question: The general solution of \(\tan\theta\tan2\theta = 1\) (found by substituting \(\tan2\theta=\tfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}\) and simplifying to \(3\tan^2\theta=1\)) is:
questions.explanation: \(3\tan^2\theta=1 \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\). \(\tan\theta=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\) gives \(\theta=n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), and \(\tan\theta=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\) gives \(\theta=n\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\); combined, \(\theta=n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{6}\).
questions.hint: Solving the reduced equation \(3\tan^2\theta=1\) gives two sign cases for \(\tan\theta\) — combine both tangent master-formula families.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the positive-root family, missing the solutions from \(\tan\theta=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\).
Applies the cosine-style \(2n\pi\pm\) spacing instead of tangent's correct \(n\pi\pm\) spacing.
Uses the wrong reference angle (\(\pi/3\) instead of the correct \(\pi/6\), since \(\tan\tfrac{\pi}{6}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\)).

questions.question: Solving \(3\tan^2\theta - (3+\sqrt3)\tan\theta + \sqrt3 = 0\), which factors as \((\tan\theta-1)(3\tan\theta-\sqrt3)=0\), the general solution is:
questions.explanation: \(\tan\theta-1=0 \Rightarrow \tan\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\). \(3\tan\theta-\sqrt3=0 \Rightarrow \tan\theta=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \Rightarrow \theta=n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{6}\). Both families together form the full solution set.
questions.hint: This is a quadratic in \(\tan\theta\) with two distinct linear factors — solve each independently and combine.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the first factor's family, missing the solutions where \(\tan\theta=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\).
Keeps only the second factor's family, missing the solutions where \(\tan\theta=1\).
Introduces a spurious \(\pm\) pattern that doesn't correspond to either factor's actual (single-family) tangent solution.

questions.question: The angle \(\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\) radians equals \(225^\circ\). Using this, the value of \(\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\) is:
questions.explanation: \(225^\circ=180^\circ+45^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III, where sine is negative: \(\sin225^\circ=-\sin45^\circ=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).
questions.hint: Convert to degrees first, then reduce to the reference angle \(45^\circ\) with the correct Quadrant III sign.
distractor_logic: Correct magnitude but wrong sign — sine is negative in Quadrant III.
This is the value of \(\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\) with the wrong sign attached, not \(\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\).
This is the value at the reference angle \(30^\circ\) rather than the correct \(45^\circ\).

questions.question: A point on the rim of a wheel of radius 12 cm sweeps through the principal-value angle solving \(2\sin\theta - 1 = 0\). The arc length swept is:
questions.explanation: The principal value satisfying \(\sin\theta=\tfrac12\) is \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}\). Then \(l=r\theta = 12\times\tfrac{\pi}{6} = 2\pi\) cm.
questions.hint: First solve the trigonometric equation for its principal value, then apply the arc-length formula with that angle (in radians).
distractor_logic: Uses half the correct radian angle (\(\pi/12\) instead of \(\pi/6\)), halving the final arc length.
Overshoots by using \(\pi/3\) instead of the correct principal value \(\pi/6\).
Reports the radius alone, without multiplying by the swept angle at all.

questions.question: If \(\sin\theta = \tfrac35\) with \(\theta\) in Quadrant II, the value of \(\sin2\theta\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos\theta=-\tfrac45\) in Quadrant II. Then \(\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 2\cdot\tfrac35\cdot\!\left(-\tfrac45\right) = -\tfrac{24}{25}\).
questions.hint: Fix the sign of cosine from the given quadrant before doubling the product.
distractor_logic: Correct magnitude but wrong sign — forgets that cosine (and hence the product) is negative in Quadrant II.
This is the value of \(\cos2\theta\), not \(\sin2\theta\).
Combines the cosine double-angle magnitude with the wrong sign as well.

questions.question: If \(\sin A=\tfrac35\) with \(A\) obtuse, and \(\cos B=\tfrac{5}{13}\) with \(B\) acute, the value of \(\sin(A-B)\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos A=-\tfrac45\) (obtuse) and \(\sin B=\tfrac{12}{13}\) (acute). Then \(\sin(A-B)=\sin A\cos B-\cos A\sin B = \tfrac35\cdot\tfrac{5}{13}-\!\left(-\tfrac45\right)\!\cdot\tfrac{12}{13} = \tfrac{15}{65}+\tfrac{48}{65}=\tfrac{63}{65}\).
questions.hint: Fix the sign of \(\cos A\) from A's quadrant before substituting into the difference formula.
distractor_logic: Uses an incorrect combination of the given values without properly deriving the missing ratios first.
Drops one of the two product terms of the difference formula.
Correct magnitude but wrong sign — the double-negative from \(-\cos A\sin B\) with \(\cos A<0\) makes this term positive, not negative overall.

questions.question: The expression \(\sin150^\circ\cos30^\circ + \cos150^\circ\sin30^\circ\), recognised as a compound-angle expansion, simplifies to:
questions.explanation: This matches \(\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B = \sin(A+B)\) with \(A=150^\circ, B=30^\circ\): \(\sin(150^\circ+30^\circ) = \sin180^\circ = 0\).
questions.hint: Recognise the compound-angle pattern first, then reduce the resulting angle using an allied-angle rule.
distractor_logic: This would follow if the two angles combined to \(90^\circ\) instead of correctly adding to \(180^\circ\).
This is \(\sin90^\circ\), corresponding to a different angle sum than the actual \(180^\circ\).
This is \(\sin270^\circ\) (an unrelated angle), not the correct sum \(180^\circ\).

questions.question: If \(\sin A = \tfrac12\) with \(A\) acute, the value of \(\sin4A\) (found via \(\sin4A = 2\sin2A\cos2A\)) is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin2A=2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(\cos2A=1-2\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac12\). Then \(\sin4A=2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) — consistent with \(A=30^\circ\Rightarrow4A=120^\circ,\ \sin120^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
questions.hint: Apply the double-angle formula twice in sequence: first to find \(\sin2A\) and \(\cos2A\), then again for \(\sin4A\).
distractor_logic: This is the given value of \(\sin A\) itself, not the result of doubling twice.
This is the value of \(\sin2A\) doubled incorrectly to \(\sin4A=1\) by simply adding instead of the proper formula.
Correct magnitude but wrong sign — \(4A=120^\circ\) lies in Quadrant II, where sine is positive, not negative.

questions.question: Using the sum-to-product formula, \(\sin4\theta + \sin2\theta\) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Using \(\sin C+\sin D=2\sin\tfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\tfrac{C-D}{2}\) with \(C=4\theta, D=2\theta\): half-sum \(=3\theta\), half-difference \(=\theta\), giving \(2\sin3\theta\cos\theta\).
questions.hint: Identify the half-sum and half-difference of the two given angles before substituting into the formula.
distractor_logic: Swaps which factor (sine vs cosine) carries the half-sum versus half-difference angle.
This is the pattern for a sum of cosines, not a sum of sines.
This is the pattern for a difference of cosines, not a sum of sines.

questions.question: Solving \(\sin\theta + \sin3\theta = 0\) by rewriting the left side as \(2\sin2\theta\cos\theta\) (via sum-to-product), the general solution is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin2\theta=0 \Rightarrow \theta=\tfrac{n\pi}{2}\) already includes every point where \(\cos\theta=0\) as well (the odd multiples of \(\pi/2\)), so the complete solution set is simply \(\theta=\tfrac{n\pi}{2}\).
questions.hint: Both factors give solutions, but check whether one family is actually already contained inside the other before combining them.
distractor_logic: Reports only every other member of the correct family, an unnecessarily restricted subset.
Reports only the subset coming from the \(\cos\theta=0\) factor, missing the (larger) family from \(\sin2\theta=0\).
Uses too fine a spacing, doubling the actual density of solutions.

questions.question: If \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant IV and \(2\sin\theta+1=0\), the value of \(\theta\) in \([0,2\pi)\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin\theta=-\tfrac12\). In Quadrant IV, this corresponds to \(\theta=2\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{6}=\tfrac{11\pi}{6}\).
questions.hint: The reference angle is \(\pi/6\); place it correctly within Quadrant IV (just before a full rotation).
distractor_logic: This is the Quadrant III solution of the same equation, not the Quadrant IV one asked for.
This is the reference-angle supplement in Quadrant II, where sine would be positive, not the required negative value.
This is just the reference angle itself, not adjusted into Quadrant IV at all.

questions.question: Expanding \(y=\sin\!\big(x+\tfrac{\pi}{3}\big)\) using the compound-angle formula gives \(y=\tfrac12\sin x+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos x\). The amplitude of this wave is:
questions.explanation: For \(y=a\sin x+b\cos x\), the amplitude is \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2} = \sqrt{\tfrac14+\tfrac34}=\sqrt1=1\) — consistent with the fact that shifting a sine wave never changes its amplitude.
questions.hint: Use \(R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) on the expanded coefficients rather than simply adding them.
distractor_logic: Reports only the coefficient of \(\sin x\) in the expansion, not the combined amplitude.
Reports only the coefficient of \(\cos x\) in the expansion, not the combined amplitude.
Adds the two coefficients directly instead of combining them as \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).

questions.question: Given \(\sin75^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\), using \(\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta\) with \(\theta=75^\circ\), the value of \(\cos150^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\sin^275^\circ = \dfrac{(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)^2}{16} = \dfrac{8+4\sqrt3}{16} = \dfrac{2+\sqrt3}{4}\). Then \(\cos150^\circ = 1-2\!\cdot\!\dfrac{2+\sqrt3}{4} = 1-\dfrac{2+\sqrt3}{2} = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), matching the direct allied-angle value.
questions.hint: Square the given radical carefully — \((\sqrt6+\sqrt2)^2\) expands to \(8+4\sqrt3\), not just \(6+2\).
distractor_logic: Forgets the cross term when squaring \((\sqrt6+\sqrt2)\), producing the wrong sign in the final subtraction.
This is the value of \(\sin150^\circ\) (a different function), not \(\cos150^\circ\).
Uses \(1-\sin^275^\circ\) (giving \(\cos^275^\circ\)) instead of \(1-2\sin^275^\circ\), missing the required factor of 2.

questions.question: For \(\theta = 220^\circ = 180^\circ+40^\circ\) (Quadrant III), the correctly-signed allied-angle reductions are:
questions.explanation: For a \(180^\circ+\theta\) shift, the function name is unchanged; the sign is fixed by Quadrant III, where tangent is positive and cosine is negative: \(\tan220^\circ=\tan40^\circ\), \(\cos220^\circ=-\cos40^\circ\).
questions.hint: Recall that for a shift by \(180^\circ\), the function name never changes — only checking Quadrant III's ASTC signs matters.
distractor_logic: Flips both signs relative to the correct pair — tangent should be positive and cosine negative in Quadrant III, not the reverse.
Incorrectly switches to co-functions (tan \(\to\) cot, cos \(\to\) sin), a rule that only applies to shifts by odd multiples of \(90^\circ\), not \(180^\circ\).
Gets tangent's sign right but cosine's sign wrong — cosine is negative, not positive, in Quadrant III.

questions.question: A point rotates with constant angular speed \(\omega=2\) rad/s starting from \(\theta=0\). At time \(t=\tfrac{\pi}{8}\) s, the value of \(\sin2\theta\) (where \(\theta=\omega t\)) is:
questions.explanation: \(\theta = \omega t = 2\times\tfrac{\pi}{8} = \tfrac{\pi}{4}\). Then \(\sin2\theta = \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\).
questions.hint: First find \(\theta\) itself from \(\theta=\omega t\), then double it before applying sine.
distractor_logic: Evaluates \(\sin\theta\) (a single, not doubled, angle) instead of the required \(\sin2\theta\).
Treats \(2\theta\) as if it were \(\pi\) rather than correctly computing \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).
An intermediate slip that neither correctly computes \(\theta\) nor \(2\theta\).

questions.question: The general solution of \(\cos\theta\cos30^\circ - \sin\theta\sin30^\circ = \tfrac12\) (recognised as \(\cos(\theta+30^\circ)=\tfrac12\)) is:
questions.explanation: With \(\alpha=\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), \(\cos\alpha=\tfrac12\) gives \(\alpha=2n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{3}\), so \(\theta = 2n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{3}-\tfrac{\pi}{6}=2n\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{6}\) or \(\theta = 2n\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{3}-\tfrac{\pi}{6}=2n\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).
questions.hint: First recognise the compound-angle pattern, then apply the cosine master formula to the shifted variable \(\theta+\pi/6\) before subtracting the shift back out.
distractor_logic: Only keeps one branch of the \(\pm\) in the cosine master formula, missing the second solution family entirely.
Applies the sine (single-family, alternating-sign) master-formula pattern instead of the correct cosine pattern.
Forgets to shift the reference angle back by \(\pi/6\) after solving for \(\alpha\), using the un-shifted reference angle directly.

questions.question: Solving \(\cos2\theta = \cos\theta\) (rewritten using \(\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1\) as \(2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1=0\), which factors as \((2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-1)=0\)), the general solution is:
questions.explanation: \(2\cos\theta+1=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-\tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta=2n\pi\pm\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\), and \(\cos\theta-1=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=2n\pi\). Both families together form the complete solution set.
questions.hint: This factored equation has two independent factors — solve each with the cosine master formula and combine.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the family from the first factor, missing the solutions where \(\cos\theta=1\).
Keeps only the family from the second factor, missing the solutions where \(\cos\theta=-\tfrac12\).
Uses tangent's \(n\pi\pm\) spacing pattern instead of the correct cosine \(2n\pi\pm\) spacing.

questions.question: The value of \(\cos20^\circ + \cos100^\circ + \cos140^\circ\) is:
questions.explanation: Group the last two terms: \(\cos100^\circ+\cos140^\circ = 2\cos120^\circ\cos20^\circ = 2\!\left(-\tfrac12\right)\!\cos20^\circ = -\cos20^\circ\). Adding the first term: \(\cos20^\circ+(-\cos20^\circ)=0\).
questions.hint: Combine the second and third terms with a sum-to-product formula first — the standard angle \(\cos120^\circ=-\tfrac12\) is what makes the whole sum collapse to zero.
distractor_logic: Stops after combining only two of the three terms, without carrying out the final cancellation with the first term.

questions.question: For \(y=\tfrac12\sin2\theta\) (equivalently \(y=\sin\theta\cos\theta\)), as \(\theta\) ranges strictly over Quadrant II (\(90^\circ<\theta<180^\circ\)), the sign of \(y\) is:
questions.explanation: For \(90^\circ<\theta<180^\circ\), \(180^\circ<2\theta<360^\circ\), an interval throughout which sine is negative (zero only at the excluded endpoints), so \(y=\tfrac12\sin2\theta\) is always negative.
questions.hint: Track the range of \(2\theta\) (not \(\theta\) itself) and check sine's sign over that doubled interval.
distractor_logic: Sine is in fact negative, not positive, throughout the open interval \((180^\circ,360^\circ)\) that \(2\theta\) sweeps through.
Zero only occurs at the excluded endpoints \(180^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\), not throughout the open interval.
Sine keeps a single, consistent (negative) sign throughout the entire open interval \((180^\circ,360^\circ)\) — it doesn't change sign partway through.

questions.question: The angle \(\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\) radians equals \(210^\circ\). The value of \(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\) is:
questions.explanation: \(210^\circ=180^\circ+30^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III, where cosine is negative: \(\cos210^\circ=-\cos30^\circ=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
questions.hint: Convert to degrees, reduce to the reference angle \(30^\circ\), then apply Quadrant III's sign for cosine.
distractor_logic: Correct magnitude but wrong sign — cosine is negative in Quadrant III.

questions.question: Using \(\sin2x\cos2x = \tfrac12\sin4x\), the period of \(y=\sin2x\cos2x\) is:
questions.explanation: Since \(y=\tfrac12\sin4x\), its period matches that of \(\sin4x\), which is \(\tfrac{2\pi}{4}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).
questions.hint: Rewrite the product as a single sine term using the double-angle identity first, then read off its period directly.
distractor_logic: This is the period of \(\sin2x\) alone, before applying the identity that doubles the effective frequency to \(\sin4x\).
This is the period of the basic, un-compressed sine function, ignoring the factor of 4 entirely.
Overstates the period by an extra factor of 2 relative to the correct \(\pi/2\).

questions.topic: Trigonometric Functions of Standard and Allied Angles
questions.question: The general solution of \(\cos\theta = \cos160^\circ\), restricted to \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\), gives the values:
questions.explanation: The master formula gives \(\theta = 360^\circ n \pm 160^\circ\); within \([0^\circ,360^\circ)\) this yields \(\theta=160^\circ\) (from \(+160^\circ\)) and \(\theta=360^\circ-160^\circ=200^\circ\) (from \(-160^\circ\), shifted by a full rotation).
questions.hint: Apply the cosine master formula, then adjust the negative branch by adding \(360^\circ\) to bring it into the required interval.
distractor_logic: Reports only the positive branch, missing the second valid solution from the negative branch.
Uses the supplementary acute angle (\(20^\circ\)) instead of correctly retaining the given obtuse reference angle throughout.
Shifts both solutions incorrectly, landing outside where the true solution pair actually falls.

questions.question: All solutions of \(2\sin x - 1 = 0\) in \([0,2\pi)\), read as the x-intercepts-style values where the graph of \(y=2\sin x-1\) crosses zero, are:
questions.explanation: \(\sin x = \tfrac12\) within one period has exactly two solutions: \(x=\tfrac{\pi}{6}\) and \(x=\pi-\tfrac{\pi}{6}=\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\).
questions.hint: Sine equals a positive value at two points per period — the reference angle itself, and \(\pi\) minus the reference angle.
distractor_logic: Misses the second solution entirely, reporting only the first-quadrant crossing.
Uses the wrong reference angle (\(\pi/3\) instead of the correct \(\pi/6\), since \(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}=\tfrac12\)).
Uses the correct reference angle but the wrong quadrant pairing — \(7\pi/6\) is where sine equals \(-\tfrac12\), not \(+\tfrac12\).

questions.question: The angle \(\tfrac{\pi}{12}\) radians equals \(15^\circ\). Using the compound-angle formula on \(45^\circ-30^\circ\), the value of \(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{12}\) is:
questions.explanation: \(\cos15^\circ = \cos45^\circ\cos30^\circ+\sin45^\circ\sin30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\).
questions.hint: First convert \(\pi/12\) to degrees, then split into \(45^\circ-30^\circ\) and apply the cosine-of-difference formula.
distractor_logic: This is the value of \(\sin15^\circ\) (using the minus sign), not \(\cos15^\circ\) — they happen to be closely related but are not identical expressions.
An expression that doesn't follow from the correct compound-angle expansion at all.
Correct numerator but the denominator is off by a factor of 2.
